birthplace: London, into the Sheridan theatrical and Whig-political family; her father was Thomas Sheridan, actor, soldier and later colonial secretary at the Cape of Good Hope, and her grandfather the playwright Richard Brinsley Sheridan
nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the Byronic lyric and the literary-annual and periodical writing of the closing Romantic decades, together with the sentimental legal-reform pamphlet literature generated by the agitation over the civil disabilities of married women
literary_identity: Poet, novelist and annual-writer who became the most publicised campaigner in England for reform of the law of infant custody and of the property and divorce rights of married women
biography: Caroline Elizabeth Sarah Sheridan was born in London on 22 March 1808, the second of three daughters of Thomas Sheridan and Caroline Henrietta Callander, herself a novelist; her grandfather was Richard Brinsley Sheridan. Thomas Sheridan died at the Cape of Good Hope in 1817 in the public service, leaving his widow nearly penniless, and the Duke of York obtained grace-and-favour apartments for the family at Hampton Court Palace. Caroline and her sisters Helen, afterwards Lady Dufferin, and Georgiana, afterwards Duchess of Somerset, were famous for beauty and wit, and she turned to writing to escape her feelings and because her family depended on her pen. On 30 June 1827 she married the Honourable George Chapple Norton, barrister and Member of Parliament for Guildford. The marriage was embittered by his violence and debts; she left him in 1836, and his criminal-conversation action against Melbourne, tried on 23 June 1836, collapsed but ruined her reputation. Under the law she lost all access to her three sons and the proceeds of her own books, and her second son William was killed by a fall from his pony in 1842. Out of that private catastrophe she made a public campaign, publishing the factory poem 'A Voice from the Factories' (1836), 'The Separation of Mother and Child by the Law of "Custody of Infants" Considered' (1838) and her 'Plain Letter to the Lord Chancellor on the Infant Custody Bill' (1839), which helped carry the Custody of Infants Act of that year. She petitioned unsuccessfully for the laureateship after Southey's death in 1843, wrote socially purposeful verse in 'The Child of the Islands' (1845), and renewed her agitation in 'English Laws for Women in the Nineteenth Century' (1854) and her 'Letter to the Queen' (1855) before the Matrimonial Causes Act of 1857. After George Norton's death in 1875 she married, on 1 March 1877, Sir William Stirling-Maxwell, an old friend; she died at her London home on 15 June 1877 and was buried in the Stirling-Maxwell vault at Lecropt church near Keir; she is now remembered as a founding figure of English marriage-law reform.
literary_profile: Norton's reputation rests on three bodies of writing. Her verse begins with 'The Sorrows of Rosalie: a Tale, with other Poems' (1829), warmly praised in 'Noctes Ambrosianae', continues with 'The Undying One and Other Poems' (1830), a romance on the Wandering Jew legend, 'The Dream and Other Poems' (1840), 'The Child of the Islands' (1845), 'Aunt Carry's Ballads for Children' (1847) and 'The Lady of La Garaye' (1862), the last thought her best by contemporaries; lyrics, ballads and metrical tales supplied the literary annuals in seasons when she is said to have earned fourteen hundred pounds. Her fiction includes 'The Wife, and Woman's Reward' (1835), 'Stuart of Dunleath' (1851), 'Lost and Saved' (1863) and 'Old Sir Douglas' (1867), the last appearing in Macmillan's Magazine. Third, and historically the most consequential, the reform prose: 'A Voice from the Factories' (1836), the custody pamphlets of 1838-9, 'English Laws for Women in the Nineteenth Century' (1854) and the letters to the Queen and on Cranworth's divorce bill of 1855-7, with much anonymous literary and artistic criticism in her later years.
stylistic_characteristics: Her manner is the Byronic one of the 1820s and 1830s: emphatic first-person remonstrance, pathos, passion, sonorous blank verse and closed couplets, and strong simple ballad stanzas for popular recitation. The Dictionary of National Biography recorded the judgement that 'she follows Byron as the dominant poet of her day', with sincere emotion but conventional expression, and that her best effects are passages of impassioned rhetoric embedded in the longer poems; 'The Lady of La Garaye' was thought to temper the Byronic note toward something like Thomas Campbell's dignity. Two lyrics, 'Joe Steel' and 'The Faded Beauty', show an arch Irish humour quite unlike her usual manner. The pamphlets are argumentative, autobiographical, pointedly domestic in their appeal to motherhood, and written to be quoted in Parliament.
intellectual_concerns: The legal non-existence of a married woman: the custody of children, the confiscation of a wife's earnings by her husband, the expense and sex-bias of the divorce court, and the exposure of a woman who defended herself in public. Her writing also holds the condition-of-England questions of the 1840s - factory labour, the education of the poor, the Prince of Wales as a national emblem - and shows her reading of Carlyle and Disraeli, while her famous refusal of the 'doctrine of equality' in 1838 marks her reform as maternal and sentimental rather than proto-feminist in the later sense. Personal grievance, evidence and petition are treated as literary instruments.
historical_significance: She converted a private scandal into a legislative campaign, and the Custody of Infants Act of 1839 gave married women for the first time a legally enforceable right to their children; her later pamphlets fed the Matrimonial Causes Act of 1857, and she is often claimed for the Married Women's Property Act of 1870, though her part in that measure is disputed. Lord Melbourne's trial and her notoriety touched the politics of the early Victorian premiership, she supplied hints for Dickens's 'Bardell v. Pickwick', she modelled for Daniel Maclise's House of Lords fresco of 'Justice', and George Meredith used her as the basis of Diana of the Crossways (1885). Modern scholarship and legal history treat her as the emblematic case of the personal made political in Victorian reform agitation.
major_influences: George Gordon Byron, Sixth Baron Byron
biographical_uncertainty: Her own later assertions are sometimes unverifiable - including her claim to have taken part in the Tolpuddle Martyrs demonstration of 1834 - and biographers differ over how far her pamphlets caused the Acts of 1839 and 1857 and over any share in the Act of 1870; no fully satisfactory portrait of her survives.

birthplace: London, in the Ponsonby circle of great Whig families; her father was Frederick Ponsonby, third earl of Bessborough, her mother Lady Henrietta Frances Spencer, daughter of John, first earl of Spencer, and her aunt by her mother's side Georgiana, Duchess of Devonshire
nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the society novel and roman a clef of the late Regency and its Byronic Gothic offshoot, written by an aristocratic salonnière who also moved in the Anglo-Irish society and politics of her father's and her husband's families
literary_identity: Novelist and occasional verse-writer of the Regency salons, remembered above all as the author of Glenarvon and as the woman who supplied the phrase and the scandal by which posterity has read Byron
biography: Caroline Ponsonby, afterwards Lady Caroline Lamb, was born on 13 November 1785, the only daughter of Frederick Ponsonby, third earl of Bessborough, by Lady Henrietta Frances Spencer, younger daughter of John, first earl of Spencer; known till 1793 as the Honourable Caroline Ponsonby. Taken to Italy at the age of three and kept there six years, she was on her return educated with her cousins at Devonshire House and then entrusted to her grandmother Lady Spencer, who was so alarmed at her eccentricities that she consulted a physician about her state of mind. On 3 June 1805 she married the Honourable William Lamb, afterwards second Viscount Melbourne and prime minister; of their children only George Augustus Frederick Lamb, born in 1807, survived, and he grew up a hopeless invalid. Byron's introduction in 1812 produced the passionate infatuation entered in her diary as 'mad, bad, and dangerous to know', and his rupture with her in 1813 made her conduct so ungovernable that her husband reluctantly prepared a deed of separation; while the legal instruments were being made ready she wrote and sent to the press 'Glenarvon', which appeared anonymously in three volumes in 1816, weeks after Byron left England. A sudden reconciliation on the day fixed for signing the deed postponed, but did not prevent, a formal separation in 1825, and her caricatures of the ton had already cost her her vouchers at Almack's. In 1819 she published anonymously the Byron imitation 'A New Canto' and canvassed the Westminster electors for her brother-in-law George Lamb; 'Graham Hamilton', sent to Colburn in 1820 with an earnest injunction not to name the author, appeared anonymously in two volumes in 1822, and 'Ada Reis; a Tale' and 'Penruddock' followed in 1823. Meeting Byron's funeral procession in July 1824 shook her afresh, and she lived chiefly at Brocket with her father-in-law and her son. She died at Melbourne House, Whitehall, on 26 January 1828, in her forty-third year and in her husband's presence, and was buried at Hatfield, having predeceased the peerage by which her name is commonly recorded.
literary_profile: Her work is almost wholly fiction and occasional verse. 'Glenarvon: A Tale' (anon., 3 vols., 1816), reprinted in one volume in 1865 as 'The Fatal Passion', is a tale of Irish rebellion and fashionable society which carries the first Byronic hero outside Byron's own poems and a self-portrait of its author as lady Adeline; the narrative poem 'A New Canto' (anon., 1819) answers 'Don Juan' in its own free manner; 'Graham Hamilton' (anon., 2 vols., 1822), whose design was said to have been suggested by Ugo Foscolo, and 'Ada Reis; a Tale' (anon., 3 vols., 1823; Paris, 1824) develop the sentimental and religious problem-novel, while 'Penruddock' (1823) turns to provincial and political life. She also wrote poetry for the literary annuals, several of her pieces being set to music by Isaac Nathan, who republished some of her verses with letters and reminiscences in 1829. Eleven of her letters survive in Lady Morgan's 'Memoirs' and seven in Paul's 'William Godwin' (1876), and her novels and poems were collected and edited by Leigh Wetherall Dickson and Paul Douglass (Pickering and Chatto, 2009).
stylistic_characteristics: Those who praised her conversation - 'full of wild originality', combining 'great and sudden contrasts' - found the same quality in her prose: rapid, rhapsodical and personal rather than crafted. The 'Monthly Review' called 'A New Canto' 'a rhapsody from beginning to end', and 'Glenarvon', which owed its brief success to its caricature portrait of Byron, was dismissed by most critics as pulp fiction while Goethe thought it worthy of serious consideration; its strength is the recognition scene and the self-dramatising heroine, its weakness unlocked emotion and a plot carried by scandal. The later fiction is more disciplined and moralised, written under Foscolo's admonition that women 'cannot afford to shock', and treats Ireland, Italy and the Catholic question as picturesque sympathy rather than argument. Salon dialogue, letter and diary aphorism remain her proper medium.
intellectual_concerns: Celebrity and its price; the power of a woman's self-portrayal in print when every character she draws is recognised; the guilt and fascination of Anglo-Irish aristocratic rule, worked out in Glenarvon's rebellion and in her own part in her husband's Irish connection; the Byronic temperament admired and reviled in the same breath; the sexual double standard of fashionable society, which excluded her after 1816 while consuming her book; and in the later novels religious faith, superstition, education and the fate of the erring woman.
historical_significance: She fixed one of the enduring images of Byron and, through 'Glenarvon', produced the first Byronic novel outside his own verse and an early and much-cited example of Irish Gothic fiction, while her roman a clef practice and her Almack's downfall made her the permanent emblem of Regency scandal. Her notoriety intersected the politics of her husband's career, and Lord Lytton, who fell briefly under her spell, used her as the original of Mrs Felix Lorraine in 'Vivian Grey' and of other of his heroines. Her diaries, letters and novels are standard sources for Byron and for the Holland House set, and modern scholarship, helped by the 2009 collected edition, has restored her from Byron anecdote to a novelist of the post-Waterloo salon and of the Irish question.
major_influences: George Gordon Byron, Sixth Baron Byron
biographical_uncertainty: The day of her birth is given by the Dictionary of National Biography and most modern accounts as 13 November 1785 but is sometimes stated as 13 January, and the day of her death variously as 25 and 26 January 1828; 'Penruddock' (1823) is attested by her modern biographer and by the collected edition but is absent from the older biographical accounts checked here; her reported attachment to the Duke of Wellington after Waterloo rests on modern biography alone; and the degree of mental illness, alcohol and laudanum dependence in her last years is judged differently by every biographer.

birthplace: Belfast, born on 10 March 1810 in the house of his maternal grandparents, the Knoxes, in High Street; his father, John Ferguson of Collon House, co. Antrim, had wasted a competence, and the family lived successively at Cider Court near Crumlin, at The Throne near Belfast and at Collon in Glenwhirry
nationality_or_literary_tradition: Irish; the Ulster Protestant and antiquarian strand of Irish Romantic writing, which made the Old Irish sagas, the Latin texts of St Patrick and the Irish song tradition the matter of a national poetry, and which looked to Scott, Burns and the metrical romance rather than to the English lake poets
literary_identity: Poet, satirist, adapter of Irish saga and song, and antiquary; a barrister who became the first Deputy Keeper of the Public Records of Ireland, was knighted, and presided over the Royal Irish Academy
biography: Samuel Ferguson, third son of John Ferguson of Collon House, co. Antrim, by Agnes Knox, was born in Belfast on 10 March 1810 in his maternal grandparents' house and grew up at Collon in Glenwhirry, where he received those impressions of nature and romance which governed his taste. His mother read aloud to the children Shakespeare, Scott, Milton, Burns, Byron, Shelley and Keats, and his father's declining means obliged him to support himself by his pen. Educated at the Belfast Academical Institution and at Trinity College Dublin, which he left, as he said, before graduation, he was called to the Irish bar in 1838, practised on the north-eastern circuit and took silk in 1859. 'The Forging of the Anchor' appeared in Blackwood's in 1832, when he was twenty-one, and was read by Professor Wilson in the 'Noctes Ambrosianae'; 'The Wet Wooing' followed, and from 1833 he was a constant contributor to the Dublin University Magazine, where 'Hibernian Nights' Entertainments' ran beside his metrical versions of Irish sagas and his 1834 attack on Hardiman's 'Irish Minstrelsy'. He versified the quarrels of the forties in 'Dublin' and 'Inheritor and Economist' (1849), and his lament for Thomas Davis, written in 1845, entered Duffy's 'Ballad Poetry of Ireland'. A founding member of Butt's Protestant Repeal Association in 1848, which he quickly left over its Young Ireland connexions, he served on the defence in John Mitchel's treason-felony trial, and on 16 August 1848 married Mary Catharine Guinness, whose North Great George's Street house drew every Dubliner who cared for letters, music or art. 'Lays of the Western Gael' (1865), 'Congal' (1872) and 'Poems' (1880), with his blank-verse 'Confession of St. Patrick' (1885), established his claim to be Ireland's national poet. First Deputy Keeper of the Public Records of Ireland from 1867, knighted in 1878 and president of the Royal Irish Academy from 1882, he died at Strand Lodge, Howth, on 9 August 1886 and was buried at Donegore; his widow's posthumous 'Ogham Inscriptions' (1887) and 'Lays of the Red Branch' (1897) fixed his standing as the forerunner of the Irish literary revival.
literary_profile: His verse, first dispersed in Blackwood's and the Dublin University Magazine, gathers the Gaelic and ecclesiastical matter of Ireland into metrical tale, lament and song: 'The Forging of the Anchor' and 'The Wet Wooing' (1832), the versions of 'O'Byrne's Bard', the 'Lament over the Ruins of Timoleague Abbey', 'The Fair Hills of Holy Ireland' and 'The Forester's Complaint' (1834), 'The Fairy Thorn' and 'Willy Gilliland' (1836), 'The Cromlech on Howth' (1841), the elegy on Thomas Davis, 'Lays of the Western Gael' (1865), 'Congal: a Poem in Five Books' (1872) on the Ulster cycle, 'Deirdre: a One-Act Drama of Old Irish Story' (1880), 'Poems' (1880), and the St Patrick translations of 1885 and 1888. In prose he wrote the mixed verse-and-tale series 'Hibernian Nights' Entertainments' (magazines 1833-6; collected 1887), the satires 'Father Tom and the Pope' (1865), 'Dublin' and 'Inheritor and Economist' (1849), and antiquarian work in the Royal Irish Academy Transactions, 'Ireland's Claims to an Adequate Parliamentary Representation of Learning' (1847), 'Our Architecture' (1867), 'Shakespearean Breviates' (1882) and the posthumous 'Ogham Inscriptions in Ireland, Wales, and Scotland' (1887).
stylistic_characteristics: Ferguson's instrument is the strong closed and heroic line of the Scottish and Augustan school, reinforced by Moore's melody and the Irish song stave, and by blank verse for saga and translation. His best effects are narrative energy and topographical exactness - the forge, the lough, the rath - rather than reflection; the ballads are plain and direct, the satires witty, colloquial and merciless, the 'Hibernian Nights' mixing prose and verse after the manner of Cowley's essays. His long versions of Irish sagas were praised by Whitley Stokes and by Judge O'Hagan, while the Dictionary of National Biography judged that, not perfectly acquainted with Irish, he sometimes gave the stories more beauties than he took away and missed something of the reality of ancient life. The poems are usually annotated, and the notes carry the antiquarian argument.
intellectual_concerns: Whether a modern Irish poetry could be built out of the Old Irish tales, the saints and the record itself, and by an Ulster Protestant voice; the ownership of Ireland's antiquities and their defence against the British Museum; the authenticity of Ossianic and fabricated Gaelic verse, tested against genuine saga and Ogham monument; the education, church and land questions of 1840s Ireland, attacked in the satires; home colonisation, industry and the dignity of labour in 'The Forging of the Anchor'; the Union, repeal and the loyalty of Protestant Ireland; and the antiquary's demand for evidence, cast, transcript and precise locality.
historical_significance: He created, before the revival, the repertory of Irish subject-matter that Yeats and Synge inherited; Yeats called him the greatest poet Ireland has produced, because the most central and most Celtic, and Lady Gregory's circle used his 'Congal' and 'Deirdre'. As first Deputy Keeper of the Public Records of Ireland he organised a department whose contents scholars had formerly misdescribed, and his Ogham corpus, published after his death with the help of Ingram, Anderson and Whitley Stokes, remained the standard collection. 'The Coolin' and 'The Lark in the Clear Air', from Gaelic originals, entered the Irish song repertory; his knighthood of 1878, his presidency of the Royal Irish Academy and his house in North Great George's Street made him the centre of Dublin literary and antiquarian life.
biographical_uncertainty: The title 'Ballads of the Fathers', named in the commission for this record, could not be found in the Dictionary of National Biography, in Lady Ferguson's biography of 1896, in the Ricorso checklists, or in the library catalogues searched, and it is therefore not listed among his works. His university career is differently reported - the Dictionary of National Biography gives him B.A. 1826, M.A. 1832 and honorary LL.D. 1864, while he himself said that he left Trinity College before graduating; 'The Forging of the Anchor' is placed in February and in May 1832 by different accounts; 'Lays of the Western Gael' was announced in November 1864 but carries the date 1865 on its title page; and 'Father Tom and the Pope', whose authorship Lady Ferguson attested, was ascribed by Yeats to William Maginn.
